newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin confident of victory in corruption fight.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin confident of victory in corruption fight.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin declared war on official corruption on Thursday and said he was sure his government would win the age-long battle against graft.
He said in a regular radio address that Russia would open up the system of tendering for state orders to reduce the temptation faced by bureaucrats and vowed to increase the authority of the state.
"I know that you will nevertheless have your doubts about our victory over corruption," Yeltsin said, speaking clearly and resolutely.
"But I am determined, I have the political will and I have your backing in this fight. I will bring this difficult struggle to an end. It will become scary to steal and to take bribes."
The 66-year-old president has made the fight against corruption a central theme of his political comeback since February after an almost eight-month absence with heart problems and pneumonia.

"Corruption is one of the main reasons that the authority of the Russian state is low today. This is preventing us from bringing order to the country and threatening the very security of Russia," he said in the radio address.

In a state of the nation speech on March 6, which paved the way for a sweeping government reshuffle that brought in or promoted a number of youthful liberals, he depicted Russian society as stagnating in bureaucratic red tape and graft that was turning people against his free market reforms.
Yeltsin also told new First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov on Wednesday that all officials should follow their honest example.

"You and I have the same credo -- not to take bribes," Yeltsin said. "He hasn't taken a kopeck and I haven't taken a kopeck," he added, referring to the subdivision of the rouble rendered obsolete by steep price rises in recent years.

Yeltsin signed a decree on Tuesday intended to reduce corruption. "By this presidential decree... we are closing all the main channels for abuse in this area," Economy Minister Yakov Urinson told Ekho Moskvy radio.
Nemtsov, 37, is to chair a meeting on Saturday that will seek to pin down details of a decree aimed at ensuring that federal contracts are filled by fair and open tender.
Sweetheart deals with federal contractors are seen as a major source of illicit income for some officials.

Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Kulikov, who is also Interior Minister and has a brief to stamp out economic crime, was quoted as saying that the decree "On Immediate Measures to Prevent Corruption" was just a partial step and a much wider document was being worked on by legal and security agencies.
Few Russians believe the administration can root out the graft that has plagued officialdom since tsarist times.
Yeltsin seems keen to show a firm hand, both to the government and to his opponents in parliament, before leaving for a holiday after an official visit to Germany next week.
On Wednesday, he accused the communist-dominated lower house of overstepping the constitution with frequent political judgements on foreign and domestic policy.

He also had strong words for the upper house, the Federation Council, where the communist lobby has been reinforced by recent local elections. "We will work together, as long as you take into account that I am the head of state," Yeltsin said.
